treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women in established preterm labour with no other risk factors.
decision_rules: Offer a choice between fetal heart rate monitoring by external cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation.
Discuss what monitoring informs at different gestational ages, including the option not to monitor when appropriate, such as at the threshold of viability.
Involve a senior obstetrician in decisions about whether and how to monitor at 23+0 to 25+6 weeks of pregnancy.

recommended_regimens.name: cardiotocography using external ultrasound
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer as one of two fetal heart rate monitoring choices when no other risk factors are present.

recommended_regimens.name: intermittent auscultation
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer as the other fetal heart rate monitoring choice when no other risk factors are present.

response_assessment.method: Interpret the cardiotocography trace if this monitoring option is used.
response_assessment.interpretation: A normal trace is reassuring; an abnormal trace does not necessarily mean fetal hypoxia or acidosis.

supportive_care: Explain the monitoring options and their limitations to the woman and, as appropriate, her family members or carers.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline states that evidence is lacking that cardiotocography improves parent or baby outcomes in preterm labour compared with intermittent auscultation. Evidence about specific monitoring features indicating hypoxia or acidosis in preterm babies is limited.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women less than 34+0 weeks pregnant for whom external cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation cannot monitor the fetal heart rate.
decision_rules: Do not use a fetal scalp electrode unless monitoring by either external method is impossible, the case has been discussed with a senior obstetrician, likely benefits outweigh potential risks, and the woman finds the discussed alternatives unacceptable.
Discuss immediate birth, intermittent ultrasound and no monitoring as alternatives.

alternative_regimens.name: fetal scalp electrode
alternative_regimens.summary: Use is permitted only when every stated exception criterion is satisfied.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: External cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation cannot monitor fetal heart rate; senior obstetrician discussion has occurred; likely benefit outweighs potential risk; and immediate birth, intermittent ultrasound and no monitoring have been discussed and are unacceptable to the woman.

not_recommended.name: fetal scalp electrode
not_recommended.reason: Do not use before 34+0 weeks unless all specified exception criteria are met.

not_recommended.name: fetal blood sampling
not_recommended.reason: Do not perform it before 34+0 weeks of pregnancy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks of pregnancy for whom external cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation cannot monitor fetal heart rate, or for whom fetal blood sampling is being considered.
decision_rules: If neither external cardiotocography nor intermittent auscultation can monitor fetal heart rate, discuss possible fetal scalp electrode use.
Discuss possible fetal blood sampling if its benefits are likely to outweigh potential risks; explain that a caesarean section is likely if a sample cannot be obtained.

alternative_regimens.name: fetal scalp electrode
alternative_regimens.summary: Discuss possible use for fetal heart rate monitoring.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: External cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation cannot monitor fetal heart rate between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks of pregnancy.

alternative_regimens.name: fetal blood sampling
alternative_regimens.summary: Discuss possible use and the likelihood of caesarean section if sampling fails.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks of pregnancy, when likely benefits outweigh potential risks.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, or with P-PROM, considering mode of birth.
decision_rules: Discuss the general and gestational-age-specific benefits and risks of vaginal and caesarean birth.
Explain the technical difficulties of preterm caesarean birth, particularly the greater likelihood of a vertical uterine (classical) incision and its implications for future pregnancies.
For women in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, explain that evidence concerning benefits or harms of caesarean birth for the baby is very limited and that none are known.
supportive_care: Include family members or carers in discussions when appropriate.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women between 26+0 and 36+6 weeks of pregnancy presenting in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour with breech presentation.
decision_rules: Consider caesarean birth for this presentation and gestational-age range.

recommended_regimens.name: caesarean birth
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider as a mode of birth for preterm labour with breech presentation, after discussing gestational-age-specific benefits and risks.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Explain the increased likelihood of a vertical uterine (classical) incision in preterm caesarean birth and its implications for future pregnancies.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Preterm babies born vaginally or by caesarean birth.
decision_rules: Wait at least 60 seconds before clamping the cord unless a specific maternal or fetal condition requires earlier clamping.
Before clamping, position the baby at or below placental level.

recommended_regimens.name: cord clamping
recommended_regimens.summary: Delay clamping as specified and position the baby at or below the placenta beforehand.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: At least 60 seconds before clamping, unless earlier clamping is required by a specific maternal or fetal condition.

artifacts.title: Selection of prophylactic vaginal progesterone or prophylactic cervical cerclage
artifacts.source_heading: 1.2 Prophylactic vaginal progesterone and prophylactic cervical cerclage
artifacts.description: Step 1: Assess whether there is a history of spontaneous preterm birth up to 34+0 weeks of pregnancy or pregnancy loss from 16+0 weeks of pregnancy onwards, and whether a transvaginal ultrasound scan performed between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks shows cervical length of 25 mm or less. Step 2: If both criteria are present, offer a choice between prophylactic vaginal progesterone and prophylactic cervical cerclage; discuss their risks and benefits and decide jointly with the woman. Step 3: If either the specified history or the specified short cervix is present, consider prophylactic vaginal progesterone. Step 4: If cervical length is 25 mm or less on a scan performed between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks and there is a history of P-PROM or cervical trauma, consider prophylactic cervical cerclage. Step 5: When vaginal progesterone is used, begin between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks and continue until at least 34 weeks. If prophylactic cervical cerclage is used, document a plan to remove the suture.
artifacts.summary: The recommendations link obstetric history and cervical length to preventive treatment choices and specify when vaginal progesterone is given. They also require a removal plan when prophylactic cerclage is used.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: These criteria distinguish when both preventive options should be offered from circumstances in which an option should be considered.

artifacts.title: Assessment of suspected P-PROM
artifacts.source_heading: 1.3 Diagnosing preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM)
artifacts.description: Step 1: If a woman reports symptoms suggestive of P-PROM, offer a speculum examination for pooling of amniotic fluid. If labour becomes established, do not perform diagnostic tests for P-PROM. Step 2: If pooling is seen, do not perform a diagnostic test; provide care consistent with P-PROM. If pooling is not seen, test vaginal fluid using insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 or placental alpha-microglobulin-1. Step 3: If the test is positive, do not determine care from that result alone. Consider the woman's clinical condition, medical and pregnancy history, and gestational age; then either provide care consistent with P-PROM or reassess diagnostic status later. Step 4: If the test is negative and no amniotic fluid is seen, do not offer antenatal prophylactic antibiotics. Explain that P-PROM is unlikely and advise reassessment if further symptoms suggest P-PROM or preterm labour. Do not use nitrazine to diagnose P-PROM.
artifacts.summary: This diagnostic sequence uses examination findings and, when needed, vaginal-fluid testing to guide assessment of suspected P-PROM. It specifies how to interpret positive and negative results without relying on a positive result alone.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The examination and test branches determine whether care should follow the P-PROM recommendations, whether later reassessment is appropriate, and when prophylactic antibiotics should not be offered.

artifacts.title: Antenatal antibiotic prophylaxis and infection assessment in P-PROM
artifacts.source_heading: 1.4 Antenatal prophylactic antibiotics for women with P-PROM; 1.5 Identifying infection in women with P-PROM
artifacts.description: Step 1: For a woman with P-PROM, offer oral erythromycin 250 mg 4 times a day to prevent intrauterine infection, for a maximum of 10 days or until established labour, whichever occurs sooner. Step 2: If erythromycin cannot be tolerated or is contraindicated, consider an oral penicillin for a maximum of 10 days or until established labour, whichever occurs sooner. Do not offer co-amoxiclav for this prophylactic purpose. Step 3: To diagnose intrauterine infection, combine clinical assessment with C-reactive protein, white blood cell count and fetal heart rate measurement by cardiotocography. Do not use any one of these tests alone to confirm or exclude infection. Step 4: If clinical findings and test results disagree, continue observation and consider repeating tests.
artifacts.summary: The sequence sets out antibiotic choices for P-PROM and the combined assessment recommended for possible intrauterine infection. It also identifies an antibiotic not to offer for prophylaxis and addresses discordant findings.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It separates infection prevention from diagnosis and prevents a single laboratory or fetal heart rate finding from being treated as decisive.

artifacts.title: Eligibility for emergency cervical cerclage
artifacts.description: Step 1: Do not offer emergency cervical cerclage if there are signs of infection, active vaginal bleeding or uterine contractions. Step 2: For a woman between 16+0 and 27+6 weeks of pregnancy with a dilated cervix and exposed, unruptured fetal membranes, consider emergency cervical cerclage. Account for gestational age, recognising that benefit is likely greater earlier in pregnancy, and for the degree of cervical dilatation; discuss the case with a consultant obstetrician and consultant paediatrician. Step 3: If considering the procedure, explain its risks and that its aim is to delay birth, increase the baby's likelihood of survival and reduce serious neonatal morbidity. Step 4: If cerclage is performed, make and document a plan for suture removal.
artifacts.summary: This pathway identifies circumstances in which emergency cerclage should not be offered and those in which it may be considered. It includes specialist discussion, counselling and planning for suture removal.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The exclusion criteria and gestational window are central to deciding whether the procedure is an appropriate option.

artifacts.title: Diagnosis of preterm labour with intact membranes
artifacts.source_heading: 1.7 Diagnosing preterm labour for women with intact membranes
artifacts.description: Step 1: Offer a clinical assessment to a woman with intact membranes who reports symptoms of preterm labour. Include history, the observations specified for initial labour assessment, and a speculum examination; follow with a digital vaginal examination if cervical dilatation cannot otherwise be assessed. If fetal fibronectin testing is anticipated, take its swab before a digital examination. Step 2: If assessment suggests suspected preterm labour at 29+6 weeks of pregnancy or less, advise treatment as described in the tocolysis and maternal corticosteroids sections. Step 3: At 30+0 weeks or more, consider transvaginal ultrasound measurement of cervical length to assess likelihood of birth within 48 hours. If length is more than 15 mm, explain that preterm labour is unlikely, consider other diagnoses, discuss discharge against continued hospital monitoring and treatment, and advise return if symptoms persist or recur. If length is 15 mm or less, treat the presentation as diagnosed preterm labour and offer treatment described in the tocolysis and maternal corticosteroids sections. Step 4: If indicated cervical-length measurement is unavailable or unacceptable at 30+0 weeks or more, consider fetal fibronectin testing instead. A negative result, concentration 50 ng/ml or less, leads to the same discussion and return advice as a cervical length of more than 15 mm. A positive result, concentration more than 50 ng/ml, leads to care for diagnosed preterm labour. Step 5: If neither test is performed at 30+0 weeks or more to exclude preterm labour, offer treatment consistent with diagnosed preterm labour. Do not combine cervical-length measurement and fetal fibronectin testing to diagnose preterm labour.
artifacts.summary: The pathway starts with clinical assessment and then branches by gestational age, cervical length or fetal fibronectin result. It also specifies management when diagnostic testing is unavailable or not performed.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The thresholds determine when to offer treatment for diagnosed preterm labour and when to discuss alternative diagnoses and possible discharge.

artifacts.title: Decision-making and treatment choices for tocolysis
artifacts.description: Step 1: Before deciding on tocolysis, consider whether labour is suspected or diagnosed, clinical features such as bleeding or infection that may make stopping labour contraindicated, gestational age, likely benefit from maternal corticosteroids, access to appropriate neonatal care and any need for transfer, and the woman's preference. Step 2: For suspected preterm labour with intact membranes between 24+0 and 25+6 weeks of pregnancy, consider nifedipine. Step 3: For suspected or diagnosed preterm labour with intact membranes between 26+0 and 33+6 weeks, offer nifedipine. Step 4: If nifedipine is contraindicated, offer oxytocin receptor antagonists. Do not offer betamimetics for tocolysis.
artifacts.summary: The pathway combines factors relevant to starting tocolysis with gestational-age-specific recommendations for nifedipine. It gives an alternative when nifedipine is contraindicated and identifies a treatment not to offer.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It distinguishes a recommendation to consider treatment from one to offer it and keeps possible contraindications within the treatment decision.

artifacts.title: Maternal corticosteroids by gestational age and prior treatment
artifacts.description: Step 1: For women between 22+0 and 23+6 weeks of pregnancy with suspected or established preterm labour, planned preterm birth or P-PROM, discuss maternal corticosteroids with the woman and the multidisciplinary team in light of individual circumstances. Step 2: For women between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks with suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, planned preterm birth or P-PROM, offer maternal corticosteroids. Step 3: For women between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks in those circumstances, consider maternal corticosteroids. Step 4: At less than 34+0 weeks, consider a single repeat course only when an earlier course was given more than 7 days ago and the risk of birth in the next 48 hours is very high. If gestation is less than 30+0 weeks or growth restriction is suspected, consider the possible effect of a repeat course on fetal growth. Step 5: Do not give more than 2 courses for preterm birth; discuss benefits and risks when offering or considering treatment.
artifacts.summary: This sequence differentiates discussion, an offer and consideration of corticosteroids across gestational ranges. It also sets conditions and a limit for repeat courses.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Gestational age, imminent birth, previous treatment and possible effects on fetal growth change the recommended corticosteroid decision.

artifacts.title: Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection
artifacts.description: Step 1: For established preterm labour or planned preterm birth within 24 hours between 23+0 and 23+6 weeks of pregnancy, discuss intravenous magnesium sulfate for the baby's neuroprotection in light of individual circumstances. Step 2: In those circumstances, offer intravenous magnesium sulfate between 24+0 and 29+6 weeks; consider it between 30+0 and 33+6 weeks. Step 3: If administered, give a 4 g intravenous bolus over 15 minutes, followed by 1 g per hour intravenously until birth or for 24 hours, whichever occurs sooner. Step 4: At least every 4 hours, record pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and deep tendon reflexes to check for magnesium toxicity. If oliguria or other evidence of renal failure occurs, increase the frequency of toxicity monitoring and reduce or stop magnesium sulfate. The guideline does not recommend use beyond 24 hours; if uncertainty about delivery timing leads to repeat administration, follow the cited MHRA safety advice.
artifacts.summary: The pathway sets gestational-age-specific decisions for neuroprotection, followed by administration and safety monitoring. It also addresses renal impairment and the guideline's limit on duration.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Eligibility depends on gestational age and likelihood of birth within 24 hours, while monitoring findings can require dose reduction or cessation.

artifacts.title: Fetal heart rate monitoring and invasive monitoring decisions
artifacts.description: Step 1: In suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, discuss the purpose and consequences of fetal monitoring and, when appropriate, the option not to monitor fetal heart rate. For women between 23+0 and 25+6 weeks, involve a senior obstetrician in deciding whether and how to monitor. Step 2: In established preterm labour without other risk factors, offer a choice between cardiotocography using external ultrasound and intermittent auscultation. Explain that evidence does not establish improved outcomes from cardiotocography compared with intermittent auscultation. Step 3: Below 34+0 weeks, do not use a fetal scalp electrode unless external cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation are both impossible, a senior obstetrician has been consulted, likely benefits outweigh potential risks, and the woman has discussed and does not accept immediate birth, intermittent ultrasound or no monitoring. Between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks, discuss possible use of a fetal scalp electrode if neither external method can monitor fetal heart rate. Step 4: Below 34+0 weeks, do not perform fetal blood sampling. Between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks, discuss its possible use if likely benefits outweigh potential risks. When offering sampling, advise that inability to obtain a sample is likely to lead to caesarean section.
artifacts.summary: This pathway covers choice of fetal monitoring and the gestational-age restrictions on a fetal scalp electrode and fetal blood sampling. It includes circumstances requiring senior obstetric input and discussion with the woman.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The decision branches distinguish routine monitoring choices from invasive approaches subject to additional conditions or restrictions.

artifacts.title: Mode-of-birth discussion in preterm labour
artifacts.description: Step 1: For suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour or P-PROM, discuss the general benefits and risks of caesarean birth and vaginal birth, as well as caesarean risks and benefits specific to gestational age. Explain the difficulty of caesarean birth for a preterm birth, particularly the greater likelihood of a vertical uterine incision and its implications for future pregnancies. Step 2: For suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, explain that no benefits or harms of caesarean birth for the baby are known, while emphasising that the evidence is very limited. Step 3: If the woman presents in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour between 26+0 and 36+6 weeks with breech presentation, consider caesarean birth.
artifacts.summary: The recommendations structure counselling about mode of birth and identify a circumstance in which caesarean birth should be considered. They preserve the stated uncertainty about outcomes for the baby.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Gestational age and breech presentation inform the birth decision, while the limited evidence and implications of uterine incision inform counselling.

recommendations.statement: Give women at increased risk of preterm labour, those with suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, and those having a planned preterm birth information and support as early as possible, according to the likelihood of preterm birth and the progress of labour. Follow NICE guidance on patient experience, recognise that the woman and her family or carers may be especially anxious, provide information both orally and in writing, describe symptoms and signs of preterm labour, and explain the care that may be offered.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.1.1 [2015]. Include family members or carers as appropriate.

recommendations.statement: For women having a planned preterm birth or offered tocolysis, maternal corticosteroids or magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection, provide information about the baby's likelihood of survival, other outcomes and risks, including long-term outcomes, using natural frequencies such as 1 in 100. Explain neonatal care and its location, immediate complications of preterm birth and possible long-term effects on growth and development. Provide repeated opportunities to discuss wishes about neonatal resuscitation, an opportunity to visit the neonatal unit, and an opportunity to speak with a neonatologist or paediatrician.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.1.2 [2015]. Include family members or carers as appropriate.

recommendations.statement: Recognise that women from some minority ethnic backgrounds or living in deprived areas may require closer monitoring and additional support because their risk of stillbirth is increased.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.1.3 [2022]. The cited 2021 MBRRACE-UK report concerned all births, not only preterm births: stillbirth rates were 32 out of 10,000 for white babies, 72 out of 10,000 for black babies and 51 out of 10,000 for Asian babies; rates were 23 out of 10,000 in the least deprived areas and 47 out of 10,000 in the most deprived areas.
recommendations.rationale: The cited report found stillbirth rates more than twice as high for black babies and around 50% higher for Asian babies than for white babies, and twice as high in the most deprived areas as in the least deprived areas.

recommendations.statement: Offer women a choice between prophylactic vaginal progesterone and prophylactic cervical cerclage when they have both a previous spontaneous preterm birth up to 34+0 weeks of pregnancy or a pregnancy loss from 16+0 weeks of pregnancy onwards, and a cervical length of 25 mm or less on transvaginal ultrasound performed between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks of pregnancy. Discuss both options' risks and benefits and decide on treatment jointly.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.2.1 [2019, amended 2022]. In April 2024, vaginal 200 mg capsules were the only progesterone preparation licensed for this indication.
recommendations.rationale: The committee found evidence that vaginal progesterone reduced preterm birth before 34 weeks in women with a prior preterm birth or a short cervix, but no evidence establishing whether it or cervical cerclage was more effective.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.2 Prophylactic vaginal progesterone and prophylactic cervical cerclage

recommendations.statement: Consider prophylactic vaginal progesterone when a woman has either a previous spontaneous preterm birth up to 34+0 weeks of pregnancy or a pregnancy loss from 16+0 weeks of pregnancy onwards, or a cervical length of 25 mm or less on transvaginal ultrasound performed between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks of pregnancy.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.2.2 [2019, amended 2022]. In April 2024, vaginal 200 mg capsules were the only progesterone preparation licensed for this indication.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence of benefit existed in groups with these risk factors, but overlapping risk factors made the benefit attributable to either factor alone uncertain.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.2 Prophylactic vaginal progesterone and prophylactic cervical cerclage

recommendations.statement: When vaginal progesterone is used, begin it between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks of pregnancy and continue it until at least 34 weeks.
recommendations.rationale: Most trials initiated treatment within the stated gestational interval; the committee's experience informed the stopping point because evidence on when to stop was absent.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.2 Prophylactic vaginal progesterone and prophylactic cervical cerclage

recommendations.statement: Consider prophylactic cervical cerclage when transvaginal ultrasound performed between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks of pregnancy shows a cervical length of 25 mm or less and the woman has either had P-PROM in a previous pregnancy or has a history of cervical trauma.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.2 Prophylactic vaginal progesterone and prophylactic cervical cerclage

recommendations.statement: If prophylactic cervical cerclage is performed, arrange and document a plan to remove the suture.
recommendations.rationale: An NHS England safety report identified instances in which cerclage sutures had not been removed.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.2 Prophylactic vaginal progesterone and prophylactic cervical cerclage

recommendations.statement: Offer a speculum examination to a woman reporting symptoms suggestive of P-PROM. If amniotic fluid is seen pooling, do not perform a diagnostic test and provide care appropriate for P-PROM. If pooling is not seen, test vaginal fluid for insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 or placental alpha-microglobulin-1.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.3 Diagnosing preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM)

recommendations.statement: After a positive insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 or placental alphamicroglobulin-1 result, do not base care solely on that result. Consider the woman's clinical condition, medical and pregnancy history, and gestational age; then either provide care appropriate for P-PROM or reassess the diagnosis later.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.3 Diagnosing preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM)

recommendations.statement: If the insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 or placental alphamicroglobulin-1 result is negative and no amniotic fluid is seen, do not give antenatal prophylactic antibiotics. Explain that P-PROM is unlikely and advise the woman to return for reassessment if further symptoms suggest P-PROM or preterm labour.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.3 Diagnosing preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM)

recommendations.statement: Do not use nitrazine to diagnose P-PROM.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.3 Diagnosing preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM)

recommendations.statement: Do not conduct diagnostic testing for P-PROM if labour becomes established in a woman who reported symptoms suggestive of P-PROM.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.3 Diagnosing preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM)

recommendations.statement: To prevent intrauterine infection in women with P-PROM, offer oral erythromycin 250 mg 4 times a day for a maximum of 10 days or until established labour begins, whichever occurs first.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.4 Antenatal prophylactic antibiotics for women with P-PROM

recommendations.statement: For women with P-PROM who cannot tolerate erythromycin or for whom it is contraindicated, consider an oral penicillin for a maximum of 10 days or until established labour begins, whichever occurs first.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.4 Antenatal prophylactic antibiotics for women with P-PROM

recommendations.statement: Do not offer co-amoxiclav to women with P-PROM as prophylaxis against intrauterine infection.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.4 Antenatal prophylactic antibiotics for women with P-PROM

recommendations.statement: For intrapartum antibiotic use, consult the relevant section of NICE's guideline on neonatal infection; where applicable, also consult its advice for women with prolonged prelabour rupture of membranes and group B streptococcal colonisation, bacteriuria or infection.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.4.4 [2015]. This recommendation refers to separate guidance rather than specifying an antibiotic regimen.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.4 Antenatal prophylactic antibiotics for women with P-PROM

recommendations.statement: Diagnose intrauterine infection in women with P-PROM using clinical assessment together with C-reactive protein, white blood cell count and fetal heart rate measurement by cardiotocography.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.5 Identifying infection in women with P-PROM

recommendations.statement: Do not rely on a single C-reactive protein test, a white blood cell count or fetal heart rate measurement by cardiotocography alone to confirm or rule out intrauterine infection in women with P-PROM.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.5 Identifying infection in women with P-PROM

recommendations.statement: If clinical findings and test results disagree, continue observing the woman and consider repeating the tests.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.5.3 [2015]; applies when assessing intrauterine infection in P-PROM.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.5 Identifying infection in women with P-PROM

recommendations.statement: Do not offer emergency cervical cerclage to women with signs of infection, active vaginal bleeding or uterine contractions.

Consider emergency cervical cerclage between 16+0 and 27+6 weeks of pregnancy when the cervix is dilated and fetal membranes are exposed but unruptured. Account for gestational age, recognising that benefit is likely greater earlier in pregnancy, and for the extent of dilatation; discuss the case with a consultant obstetrician and a consultant paediatrician.
When considering emergency cervical cerclage, explain its risks and its aim of delaying birth to improve the baby's chance of survival and reduce serious neonatal morbidity.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.6.3 [2015, amended 2022]. Include family members or carers as appropriate.

recommendations.statement: If emergency cervical cerclage is performed, arrange and document a plan for removing the suture.
recommendations.rationale: An NHS England safety report described instances in which cerclage sutures were not removed.

recommendations.statement: Explain to women reporting preterm labour symptoms with intact membranes which clinical assessments and diagnostic tests are available, how they are performed, and their benefits, risks and possible consequences. Include the implications of false-positive and false-negative results in light of gestational age.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.7.1 [2015]. Include family members or carers as appropriate.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.7 Diagnosing preterm labour for women with intact membranes

recommendations.statement: Offer women reporting preterm labour symptoms with intact membranes a clinical assessment comprising a clinical history, the initial labour observations described in NICE's intrapartum care guideline, and a speculum examination. Follow with a digital vaginal examination if cervical dilatation cannot otherwise be assessed; if fetal fibronectin sampling is anticipated, obtain the swab before any digital examination.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.7 Diagnosing preterm labour for women with intact membranes

recommendations.statement: If assessment indicates suspected preterm labour at 29+6 weeks of pregnancy or less, advise treatment for preterm labour as set out in the tocolysis and maternal corticosteroids sections.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.7.3 [2015]; applies to women with intact membranes.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.7 Diagnosing preterm labour for women with intact membranes

recommendations.statement: For suspected preterm labour at 30+0 weeks of pregnancy or more, consider transvaginal ultrasound cervical-length measurement to assess the likelihood of birth within 48 hours. If the cervix measures more than 15 mm, explain that preterm labour is unlikely, consider other diagnoses, discuss discharge versus hospital monitoring and treatment, and advise return if symptoms persist or recur after discharge. If it measures 15 mm or less, regard preterm labour as diagnosed and offer treatment according to the tocolysis and maternal corticosteroids sections.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.7.4 [2015]; applies to women with intact membranes.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.7 Diagnosing preterm labour for women with intact membranes

recommendations.statement: At 30+0 weeks of pregnancy or more, consider fetal fibronectin testing to assess the likelihood of birth within 48 hours if cervical-length ultrasound is indicated but unavailable or unacceptable. With a negative result (concentration 50 ng/ml or less), explain that preterm labour is unlikely, consider other diagnoses, discuss discharge versus continued hospital monitoring and treatment, and advise return if symptoms persist or recur after discharge. With a positive result (concentration more than 50 ng/ml), regard preterm labour as diagnosed and offer treatment according to the tocolysis and maternal corticosteroids sections.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.7.5 [2015]; applies to women with intact membranes.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.7 Diagnosing preterm labour for women with intact membranes

recommendations.statement: If a woman with suspected preterm labour at 30+0 weeks of pregnancy or more has neither cervical-length ultrasound nor fetal fibronectin testing to exclude preterm labour, offer treatment as for diagnosed preterm labour, following the tocolysis and maternal corticosteroids sections.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.7 Diagnosing preterm labour for women with intact membranes

recommendations.statement: Do not combine transvaginal ultrasound cervical-length measurement with fetal fibronectin testing to diagnose preterm labour.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.7 Diagnosing preterm labour for women with intact membranes

recommendations.statement: Have cervical-length transvaginal ultrasound scans performed by healthcare professionals trained and experienced in this measurement.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.7 Diagnosing preterm labour for women with intact membranes

recommendations.statement: For other biomarker tests used to diagnose preterm labour, consult NICE's diagnostics guidance on biomarker tests for women with intact membranes.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.7.9 [2019]. This recommendation directs readers to separate guidance.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.7 Diagnosing preterm labour for women with intact membranes

recommendations.statement: When deciding whether to start tocolysis, consider whether preterm labour is suspected or diagnosed, clinical features such as bleeding or infection that may contraindicate stopping labour, gestational age, likely benefit from maternal corticosteroids, availability of suitable neonatal care and any need for transfer, and the woman's preference.
Consider nifedipine for tocolysis between 24+0 and 25+6 weeks of pregnancy when membranes are intact and preterm labour is suspected.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.8.2 [2015]. This use of nifedipine was off label in November 2015.

recommendations.statement: Offer nifedipine for tocolysis between 26+0 and 33+6 weeks of pregnancy when membranes are intact and preterm labour is suspected or diagnosed.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.8.3 [2015]. This use of nifedipine was off label in November 2015.

recommendations.statement: If nifedipine is contraindicated, offer oxytocin receptor antagonists for tocolysis.
Do not offer betamimetics for tocolysis.

For women between 22+0 and 23+6 weeks of pregnancy with suspected or established preterm labour, a planned preterm birth or P-PROM, discuss maternal corticosteroid use with the woman and the multidisciplinary team in light of her individual circumstances.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.9.1 [2015, amended 2022]. Include family members or carers as appropriate. The guideline states that use of betamethasone and dexamethasone was off label in June 2022.

recommendations.statement: Offer maternal corticosteroids between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks of pregnancy to women with suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, a planned preterm birth or P-PROM.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.9.2 [2015, amended 2019]. The guideline states that use of betamethasone and dexamethasone was off label in June 2022.

recommendations.statement: Consider maternal corticosteroids between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks of pregnancy for women with suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, a planned preterm birth or P-PROM.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.9.3 [2015]. The guideline states that use of betamethasone and dexamethasone was off label in June 2022.

recommendations.statement: Consider a single repeat course of maternal corticosteroids before 34+0 weeks of pregnancy if the previous course was more than 7 days ago and birth is very likely within the next 48 hours. If the woman is less than 30+0 weeks pregnant or fetal growth restriction is suspected, consider the repeat course's possible effect on fetal growth.
recommendations.rationale: The committee considered that one repeat course may help when preterm birth is imminent, while noting evidence of reduced birthweight after repeat dosing and uncertainty about longer-term outcomes.

recommendations.statement: Do not give more than 2 courses of maternal corticosteroids for preterm birth.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.9.5 [2022]. The committee clarified that courses given for other reasons during pregnancy do not count towards this limit.
recommendations.rationale: The committee judged that birthweight effects from multiple repeat courses may outweigh their benefits.

recommendations.statement: Discuss the benefits and risks with the woman whenever maternal corticosteroids are offered or considered.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.9.6 [2015, amended 2022]. Include family members or carers as appropriate.
recommendations.rationale: The committee identified potential benefit from repeat treatment alongside concerns about birthweight and uncertainty about longer-term outcomes.

recommendations.statement: For corticosteroid use in people with diabetes, consult NICE's guideline on diabetes in pregnancy.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.9.7 [2019]. This recommendation directs readers to separate guidance.

recommendations.statement: For women between 23+0 and 23+6 weeks of pregnancy in established preterm labour or expecting a planned preterm birth within 24 hours, discuss intravenous magnesium sulfate for neonatal neuroprotection in light of individual circumstances.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.10.1 [2019]. Include family members or carers as appropriate. This intravenous use was off label in August 2019.

recommendations.statement: Offer intravenous magnesium sulfate for neonatal neuroprotection between 24+0 and 29+6 weeks of pregnancy when the woman is in established preterm labour or a planned preterm birth is expected within 24 hours.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.10.2 [2015]. This intravenous use was off label in August 2019.

recommendations.statement: Consider intravenous magnesium sulfate for neonatal neuroprotection between 30+0 and 33+6 weeks of pregnancy when the woman is in established preterm labour or a planned preterm birth is expected within 24 hours.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.10.3 [2015]. This intravenous use was off label in August 2019.

recommendations.statement: Administer magnesium sulfate as a 4 g intravenous bolus over 15 minutes, then infuse intravenously at 1 g per hour until birth or for 24 hours, whichever occurs first.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.10.4 [2015]. The guideline does not recommend magnesium sulfate use beyond 24 hours; if uncertainty about birth timing leads to repeat administration, it directs readers to MHRA safety advice.

recommendations.statement: While a woman receives magnesium sulfate, assess for clinical signs of magnesium toxicity at least every 4 hours, recording pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and deep tendon reflexes, such as patellar reflexes.
If oliguria or other evidence of renal failure is present or develops during magnesium sulfate treatment, monitor more frequently for magnesium toxicity and reduce or stop magnesium sulfate.
For intrapartum antibiotic use during established preterm labour, consult NICE's guideline on neonatal infection.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.11.1 [2019]. This recommendation directs readers to separate guidance.

recommendations.statement: Discuss the purpose and process of fetal monitoring with women in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, including the decisions it informs at different gestational ages and, where appropriate, the option of not monitoring fetal heart rate, such as at the threshold of viability.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.12.1 [2015]. Include family members or carers as appropriate.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.12 Fetal monitoring — Monitoring options: cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation

recommendations.statement: Include a senior obstetrician in discussions about whether and how to monitor fetal heart rate between 23+0 and 25+6 weeks of pregnancy.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.12 Fetal monitoring — Monitoring options: cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation

recommendations.statement: Explain fetal monitoring options, noting that evidence is limited on which specific findings indicate hypoxia or acidosis in preterm babies, although available evidence broadly agrees with that for term babies. Explain that a normal cardiotocography trace is reassuring about the baby's response to labour, whereas an abnormal trace does not necessarily mean fetal hypoxia or acidosis.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.12.3 [2015]. Include family members or carers as appropriate.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.12 Fetal monitoring — Monitoring options: cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation

recommendations.statement: Explain that evidence is absent that cardiotocography, compared with intermittent auscultation, improves outcomes of preterm labour for the parent or baby.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.12.4 [2015]. Include family members or carers as appropriate.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.12 Fetal monitoring — Monitoring options: cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation

recommendations.statement: In established preterm labour without other risk factors, offer a choice between fetal heart rate monitoring by cardiotocography using external ultrasound and intermittent auscultation.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.12 Fetal monitoring — Monitoring options: cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation

recommendations.statement: For instructions on intermittent auscultation to monitor fetal heart rate, consult NICE's guideline on fetal monitoring in labour.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.12.6 [2015]. This recommendation directs readers to separate guidance.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.12 Fetal monitoring — Monitoring options: cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation

recommendations.statement: Before 34+0 weeks of pregnancy, do not use a fetal scalp electrode unless external cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation are both infeasible, the issue has been discussed with a senior obstetrician, benefits are likely to exceed potential risks, and immediate birth, intermittent ultrasound and no monitoring have been discussed with the woman and are unacceptable to her.
Between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks of pregnancy, discuss possible fetal scalp electrode use when fetal heart rate cannot be monitored by external cardiotocography or intermittent auscultation.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.12.8 [2015]. Include family members or carers as appropriate.

recommendations.statement: Do not perform fetal blood sampling before 34+0 weeks of pregnancy.
Between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks of pregnancy, discuss possible fetal blood sampling with the woman if its benefits are likely to outweigh its potential risks.

When offering fetal blood sampling, advise the woman that caesarean section is likely if a sample cannot be obtained; also consult the fetal blood sampling advice in the relevant NICE intrapartum care guidelines.
Discuss the general benefits and risks of caesarean birth and vaginal birth with women in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour or with P-PROM.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.13.1 [2015]. Include family members or carers as appropriate; the guideline also refers to NICE advice on planning mode of birth.

recommendations.statement: Explain gestational-age-specific benefits and risks of caesarean birth to women in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour or with P-PROM. In particular, explain the procedural difficulties of preterm caesarean birth, the increased likelihood of a vertical uterine (classical) incision and the consequences for future pregnancies.
Explain to women in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour that no benefits or harms of caesarean birth for the baby are known, while emphasising that the evidence is very limited.
Consider caesarean birth for women presenting in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour between 26+0 and 36+6 weeks of pregnancy when the baby is in breech presentation.
Delay clamping a preterm baby's umbilical cord for at least 60 seconds unless a specific maternal or fetal condition requires earlier clamping.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.14.1 [2015, amended 2022]. Applies after vaginal or caesarean birth.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.14 Timing of cord clamping for preterm babies (born vaginally or by caesarean birth)

recommendations.statement: Before clamping the cord, place the preterm baby at or below placental level.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.14.2 [2015]. Applies after vaginal or caesarean birth.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.14 Timing of cord clamping for preterm babies (born vaginally or by caesarean birth)

document_sections.heading: Overview
document_sections.content: The guideline addresses care for people with a singleton pregnancy who are at increased risk of preterm labour, have symptoms or signs of labour before 37 weeks, or are having a planned preterm birth. Its aims are to reduce risks to the baby and describe interventions that prevent or delay early labour and birth. The terms 'woman' and 'mother' also include pregnant people and people who have given birth who do not identify as women.

document_sections.heading: Who is it for?
document_sections.content: The intended audience includes healthcare professionals caring for these pregnancies; commissioners and providers of maternity services; and affected women, their families and carers.

document_sections.heading: 1.1 Information and support
document_sections.content: Give information and support as early as possible to women at increased risk of preterm labour, with suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, or having a planned preterm birth. Take account of the likelihood of birth and the stage of labour, follow the principles of NICE's guideline on patient experience in adult NHS services, recognise possible anxiety, provide spoken and written information, describe signs and symptoms, and explain potential care. For women having a planned preterm birth or offered tocolysis, maternal corticosteroids or magnesium sulfate, explain the baby's likelihood of survival, other outcomes and risks, including long-term outcomes, using natural frequencies such as 1 in 100. Describe where and how neonatal care will be provided, immediate problems after preterm birth and possible long-term effects on growth and development. Provide continuing opportunities to express wishes about neonatal resuscitation, visit the neonatal unit and speak with a neonatologist or paediatrician. Include family members or carers when appropriate. The 2021 MBRRACE-UK report indicates that some minority ethnic groups and people living in deprived areas have higher stillbirth risks and may require closer monitoring and extra support. Its figures concern all births, not only preterm births: stillbirth occurred in 32 out of 10,000 white babies, 72 out of 10,000 black babies, a rate more than twice as high, and 51 out of 10,000 Asian babies, a rate around 50% higher. Rates were 23 out of 10,000 in the least deprived areas and 47 out of 10,000 in the most deprived areas, approximately twice as high in the latter.

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Prophylactic vaginal progesterone and prophylactic cervical cerclage
document_sections.content: Offer a choice between prophylactic vaginal progesterone and prophylactic cervical cerclage when both criteria are present: previous spontaneous preterm birth up to 34+0 weeks of pregnancy or pregnancy loss from 16+0 weeks of pregnancy onwards, and cervical length of 25 mm or less on transvaginal ultrasound between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks of pregnancy. Discuss each option's benefits and risks and decide jointly. Consider prophylactic vaginal progesterone if either that obstetric history or that ultrasound finding is present. In April 2024, vaginal 200 mg capsules were the only progesterone preparation licensed for this indication. Start vaginal progesterone between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks of pregnancy and continue to at least 34 weeks. Consider prophylactic cervical cerclage when cervical length is 25 mm or less on a scan between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks of pregnancy and there is either previous preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM) or a history of cervical trauma. If cerclage is performed, establish and document a suture-removal plan.

document_sections.heading: 1.3 Diagnosing preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM)
document_sections.content: For symptoms suggestive of P-PROM, offer speculum examination to assess for pooled amniotic fluid. If fluid is seen, do not perform another diagnostic test; provide care on the basis that P-PROM is present. If no pooling is seen, test vaginal fluid for insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 or placental alpha-microglobulin-1. A positive result alone must not determine care: also assess clinical condition, medical and pregnancy history, and gestational age, then either provide P-PROM care or reassess diagnostic status later. If the test is negative and no amniotic fluid is seen, do not offer antenatal prophylactic antibiotics; explain that P-PROM is unlikely and advise reassessment if suggestive symptoms of P-PROM or preterm labour arise again. Do not use nitrazine to diagnose P-PROM. Do not test for P-PROM once labour is established in someone reporting suggestive symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 1.4 Antenatal prophylactic antibiotics for women with P-PROM
document_sections.content: To prevent intrauterine infection in women with P-PROM, offer oral erythromycin 250 mg 4 times a day for a maximum of 10 days or until established labour, whichever occurs first. If erythromycin cannot be tolerated or is contraindicated, consider an oral penicillin for the same maximum duration or until established labour, whichever occurs first. Do not offer co-amoxiclav for this prophylactic purpose. For intrapartum antibiotic decisions, consult NICE's guideline on neonatal infection, including its guidance for prolonged prelabour rupture of membranes with group B streptococcal colonisation, bacteriuria or infection when relevant.

document_sections.heading: 1.5 Identifying infection in women with P-PROM
document_sections.content: Diagnose intrauterine infection using clinical assessment together with C-reactive protein, white blood cell count and fetal heart rate measured by cardiotocography. No single C-reactive protein result, white blood cell count or cardiotocography assessment should independently confirm or exclude infection. If clinical findings and test results disagree, continue observation and consider repeating tests.

document_sections.heading: 1.6 Emergency cervical cerclage
document_sections.content: Do not offer emergency cervical cerclage when infection signs, active vaginal bleeding or uterine contractions are present. Consider it between 16+0 and 27+6 weeks of pregnancy for a dilated cervix with exposed but unruptured fetal membranes. Weigh gestational age, noting that benefit is likely greater earlier, and the degree of dilatation; discuss the case with a consultant obstetrician and consultant paediatrician. If considering the procedure, explain its risks and its aim of postponing birth to improve the baby's chance of survival and reduce serious neonatal morbidity. If performed, make and document a plan to remove the suture.

document_sections.heading: 1.7 Diagnosing preterm labour for women with intact membranes
document_sections.content: Explain available clinical assessment and diagnostic tests to women with symptoms and intact membranes, including how they are done and their benefits, risks and possible consequences, particularly false-positive and false-negative findings in relation to gestational age. Offer assessment comprising clinical history, observations specified in NICE's guideline on intrapartum care and speculum examination. Follow with digital vaginal examination if cervical dilatation cannot otherwise be assessed; collect any anticipated fetal fibronectin swab before digital examination. If assessment suggests preterm labour at 29+6 weeks of pregnancy or less, advise treatment as described under tocolysis and maternal corticosteroids. At 30+0 weeks of pregnancy or more, consider transvaginal cervical-length ultrasound to estimate likelihood of birth within 48 hours. A length of more than 15 mm makes preterm labour unlikely: consider alternative diagnoses, discuss discharge versus hospital monitoring and treatment, and advise return if symptoms persist or recur. A length of 15 mm or less establishes diagnosed preterm labour for care purposes; offer the described treatment. If that ultrasound is indicated but unavailable or unacceptable at 30+0 weeks or more, consider fetal fibronectin testing to assess likelihood of birth within 48 hours. A negative concentration of 50 ng/ml or less makes preterm labour unlikely and calls for the same discussion of alternatives, discharge and return precautions. A positive concentration of more than 50 ng/ml warrants treating the woman as having diagnosed preterm labour. If neither test is performed to exclude preterm labour at 30+0 weeks or more, offer care consistent with diagnosed preterm labour. Do not combine cervical-length ultrasound and fetal fibronectin testing for diagnosis. Cervical-length scans should be performed by professionals trained and experienced in that measurement. NICE's separate diagnostics guidance addresses other biomarker tests.

document_sections.heading: 1.8 Tocolysis
document_sections.content: When deciding whether to begin tocolysis, consider whether labour is suspected or diagnosed, clinical features such as bleeding or infection that may contraindicate stopping labour, gestational age, likely benefit from maternal corticosteroids, access to appropriate neonatal care if transfer is needed, and the woman's preference. Consider nifedipine at 24+0 to 25+6 weeks of pregnancy when membranes are intact and preterm labour is suspected. Offer nifedipine at 26+0 to 33+6 weeks of pregnancy with intact membranes and suspected or diagnosed preterm labour. Both uses of nifedipine were off-label in November 2015. If nifedipine is contraindicated, offer oxytocin receptor antagonists. Do not offer betamimetics for tocolysis.

document_sections.heading: 1.9 Maternal corticosteroids
document_sections.content: Use of betamethasone and dexamethasone in this setting was off-label in June 2022. At 22+0 to 23+6 weeks of pregnancy, discuss maternal corticosteroids with the woman and multidisciplinary team in light of individual circumstances if preterm labour is suspected or established, preterm birth is planned, or P-PROM is present. Offer maternal corticosteroids at 24+0 to 33+6 weeks of pregnancy for suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, planned preterm birth or P-PROM. Consider them for the same situations at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks of pregnancy. Consider one repeat course before 34+0 weeks of pregnancy only when a previous course was given more than 7 days ago and birth in the next 48 hours is very likely. If gestation is less than 30+0 weeks or growth restriction is suspected, consider the potential effect of repetition on fetal growth. Do not give more than 2 courses for preterm birth. Discuss benefits and risks whenever offering or considering treatment. NICE's guideline on diabetes in pregnancy addresses corticosteroid use in people with diabetes.

document_sections.heading: 1.10 Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection
document_sections.content: Intravenous magnesium sulfate for the specified neuroprotection indications was off-label in August 2019. The guideline does not recommend its use beyond 24 hours; if uncertainty about delivery timing leads to repeated administration, follow MHRA safety advice. At 23+0 to 23+6 weeks of pregnancy, discuss its use in individual circumstances if labour is established or planned birth will occur within 24 hours. Offer it at 24+0 to 29+6 weeks of pregnancy for established labour or planned birth within 24 hours; consider it under those circumstances at 30+0 to 33+6 weeks. Administer a 4 g intravenous bolus over 15 minutes, then infuse 1 g per hour until birth or for 24 hours, whichever is sooner. At least every 4 hours, check pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and deep tendon reflexes for toxicity. With existing or developing oliguria or other evidence of renal failure, monitor toxicity more frequently and reduce or stop magnesium sulfate.

document_sections.heading: 1.11 Intrapartum antibiotics
document_sections.content: For intrapartum antibiotic use during established preterm labour, consult NICE's guideline on neonatal infection.

document_sections.heading: Monitoring options: cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation
document_sections.content: Discuss the purpose and process of fetal monitoring, the decisions it supports at different gestational ages and, where appropriate, the option of no fetal heart rate monitoring, such as at the threshold of viability. Involve a senior obstetrician in decisions about whether and how to monitor at 23+0 to 25+6 weeks of pregnancy. Explain monitoring choices while acknowledging limited evidence on which specific features indicate hypoxia or acidosis in preterm babies; available evidence broadly accords with that for babies born at term. A normal cardiotocography trace is reassuring, whereas an abnormal one does not necessarily mean fetal hypoxia or acidosis. Explain that evidence is absent that cardiotocography improves outcomes for the parent or baby compared with intermittent auscultation in preterm labour. In established preterm labour without other risk factors, offer a choice of external-ultrasound cardiotocography or intermittent auscultation. NICE's guideline on fetal monitoring in labour provides instructions for intermittent auscultation. Include family members or carers in discussions when appropriate.

document_sections.heading: Fetal scalp electrode
document_sections.content: Before 34+0 weeks of pregnancy, do not use a fetal scalp electrode unless external cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation are both impossible, a senior obstetrician has been consulted, likely benefits exceed potential risks, and the woman finds the discussed alternatives of immediate birth, intermittent ultrasound and no monitoring unacceptable. At 34+0 to 36+6 weeks of pregnancy, discuss possible electrode use if neither external cardiotocography nor intermittent auscultation can monitor the fetal heart rate.

document_sections.heading: Fetal blood sampling
document_sections.content: Do not perform fetal blood sampling before 34+0 weeks of pregnancy. At 34+0 to 36+6 weeks, discuss its possible use if benefits are likely to exceed potential risks. When offering it, explain that failure to obtain a sample is likely to lead to caesarean section. NICE's intrapartum-care guidelines provide additional advice.

document_sections.heading: 1.13 Mode of birth
document_sections.content: Discuss general benefits and risks of vaginal and caesarean birth with women in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour or with P-PROM. Explain gestational-age-specific benefits and risks of caesarean birth, particularly the technical difficulty of preterm caesarean birth, the greater likelihood of a vertical uterine (classical) incision and implications for later pregnancies. Explain that no benefits or harms to the baby from caesarean birth are known, while emphasising that evidence is very limited. Consider caesarean birth for breech presentation with suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour at 26+0 to 36+6 weeks of pregnancy.

document_sections.heading: 1.14 Timing of cord clamping for preterm babies (born vaginally or by caesarean birth)
document_sections.content: Wait at least 60 seconds before clamping a preterm baby's cord unless specific maternal or fetal circumstances require earlier clamping. Before clamping, place the baby at or below placental level.

document_sections.heading: Cervical trauma
document_sections.content: The term includes physical cervical injury and surgery, including previous cone biopsy by cold knife or laser, large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ; any number), or radical diathermy.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosed preterm labour
document_sections.content: This means suspected preterm labour accompanied by a positive diagnostic test for preterm labour.

document_sections.heading: Emergency cervical cerclage (previously known as 'rescue')
document_sections.content: This is cerclage performed urgently for premature cervical dilatation, frequently when fetal membranes are exposed.

document_sections.heading: Established preterm labour
document_sections.content: This is regular contractions accompanied by progressive cervical dilatation from 4 cm.

document_sections.heading: MBRRACE-UK
document_sections.content: Mothers and babies: reducing risk through audits and confidential enquiries across the UK (MBRRACE-UK) comprises audits intended to identify causes of maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity and inform maternity-care recommendations to reduce these outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM)
document_sections.content: P-PROM means membrane rupture before 37+0 weeks of pregnancy without established labour.

document_sections.heading: Suspected preterm labour
document_sections.content: This describes reported preterm-labour symptoms followed by clinical assessment, including speculum or digital vaginal examination, that finds preterm labour possible but excludes established labour.

document_sections.heading: Symptoms of preterm labour
document_sections.content: This describes presentation before 37+0 weeks of pregnancy with potentially suggestive symptoms, such as abdominal pain, before any clinical assessment involving speculum or digital vaginal examination.

document_sections.heading: 1 Repeating maternal corticosteroids
document_sections.content: The committee proposes research comparing one repeat dose or one repeat course (2 doses) with a single course for preterm neonatal and longer-term child outcomes. It also asks for the optimal interval between completion of the initial course (2 doses) and repetition.

document_sections.heading: 2 Prophylactic vaginal progesterone
document_sections.content: The research question is whether progesterone lowers preterm-birth risk when risk factors are present but cervical length is more than 25 mm.

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: Preterm birth causes substantial morbidity for women and babies, harms families and generates NHS costs. Evidence supports progesterone for lowering preterm-birth risk, but studies enrolled women with combinations of risk factors, including previous preterm birth and a short cervix. Evidence of effectiveness is absent for women with other risk factors but without a short cervix. Consequently, whether to recommend progesterone in this group, and whether cervical-length measurement is necessary to guide treatment, remains difficult to determine.

document_sections.heading: 3 Prophylactic vaginal progesterone
document_sections.content: The research question is whether progesterone lowers preterm-birth risk when cervical length is 25 mm or less but other preterm-birth risk factors are absent.

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: Preterm birth substantially affects maternal and infant health, families and NHS expenditure. Evidence favours progesterone for reducing preterm birth, but studies include people with overlapping risk factors such as previous preterm birth and a shortened cervix. Effectiveness evidence is lacking for a cervical length of 25 mm or less without other risk factors. This leaves uncertainty about recommending treatment and about the need to measure cervical length to guide care for women with no other risk factors.

document_sections.heading: 4 Prophylactic vaginal progesterone
document_sections.content: The committee asks which gestational ages are optimal for starting and stopping prophylactic vaginal progesterone.

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: Preterm birth causes considerable morbidity for women and babies, adversely affects families and costs the NHS. Although evidence indicates that progesterone reduces preterm birth, studies have not established the best gestational ages for initiating and ending treatment. Therefore, the ideal starting point and duration remain uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 5 Prophylactic vaginal progesterone and prophylactic cervical cerclage
document_sections.content: The proposed research compares prophylactic cervical cerclage alone, prophylactic vaginal progesterone alone and both together for preventing preterm birth in women with a short cervix and previous spontaneous preterm birth.

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: Preterm birth causes substantial neonatal mortality, morbidity and long-term disability. Recognised risk factors permit preventive interventions. Both prophylactic cervical cerclage and prophylactic vaginal progesterone are effective in women with a short cervix and a history of preterm birth, but comparative effectiveness and relative benefits, risks and costs have limited evidence. Further randomised research comparing maternal and neonatal outcomes could help women and professionals choose prophylaxis.

document_sections.heading: 6 Identifying infection in women with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM)
document_sections.content: The committee asks how accurately serial C-reactive protein testing identifies chorioamnionitis in women with P-PROM.

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: Recognising infection in P-PROM supports appropriate care and may permit consideration of antibiotics or early birth. Effective infection treatment matters because sepsis is a common direct cause of maternal death. Evidence that serial C-reactive protein testing may help is currently limited, although the committee knows it is commonly used. Diagnostic studies are needed to assess accuracy for chorioamnionitis, a common and serious infectious complication of P-PROM.

document_sections.heading: 7 Emergency cervical cerclage
document_sections.content: The proposed research asks whether emergency cerclage improves outcomes in women at risk of preterm birth.

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: Some randomised-study evidence suggests emergency cerclage may improve neonatal outcomes with cervical dilatation and exposed, intact membranes, but the size of any effect is uncertain. Its full consequences and which subgroups benefit most are unknown. A randomised controlled trial would best answer the question; a national registry recording neonatal mortality and morbidity and maternal morbidity could also be considered for women who decline trial participation but choose 'rescue' cerclage.

document_sections.heading: 8 Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection
document_sections.content: The research question compares a magnesium sulfate bolus followed by infusion with a bolus alone for preventing neurodevelopmental injury in babies born preterm.

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: Randomised studies provide evidence of neonatal neuroprotection when magnesium sulfate is given to women delivering preterm up to 34+0 weeks of pregnancy. The best administration strategy remains uncertain because studies have used different approaches. A bolus alone would benefit women and reduce healthcare costs if equally effective: magnesium sulfate has maternal side effects, while infusion needs additional monitoring and associated expenditure. A randomised controlled trial could compare neonatal and maternal outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Prophylactic vaginal progesterone
document_sections.content: The rationale and impact discussion concerns recommendations 1.2.1 to 1.2.5.

document_sections.heading: Why the committee made the recommendations
document_sections.content: Good evidence showed that vaginal progesterone reduced births before 34 weeks among women with previous preterm birth and among those with cervical length of 25 mm or less. Because these groups overlap, the committee retained an offer of progesterone for women with both factors and made it an equal option to cervical cerclage; no new cerclage evidence review had been undertaken, and evidence does not establish which option works better. The differing treatment burdens—regular vaginal treatment throughout pregnancy versus one operation—support shared discussion of benefits and risks. The committee noted uncertainty about which risk factors should identify women for treatment, including cervical length, previous preterm birth and cervical surgery. Cervical scanning varies across the country and is offered for clinical concern rather than routinely. Progesterone may reduce preterm birth for some risk profiles but not others. Overlapping risk factors make it hard to determine which individual factor identifies women who definitely benefit; the committee therefore recommended considering progesterone when either previous preterm birth or cervical length of 25 mm or less is present. Uncertainty for women with only one of these factors prompted research recommendations. Treatment-start timing varied across studies, although most trials began between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks; this aligned with committee experience. Evidence did not identify when to stop treatment, so the recommendation to continue until at least 34 weeks relied on committee experience, and optimal timing remains a research question. A report by NHS England of instances in which cerclage sutures were not removed prompted the requirement for a documented removal plan.

document_sections.heading: How the recommendations might affect practice
document_sections.content: Vaginal progesterone is commonly used and relatively inexpensive, so major practice change is not expected. Considering it for women with previous preterm birth despite unknown cervical length or a measured length greater than 25 mm may increase its use; fewer preterm births are likely to generate overall savings. Planning removal of prophylactic cerclage sutures is not expected to change practice.

document_sections.heading: Emergency cervical cerclage
document_sections.content: The rationale and impact discussion concerns recommendation 1.6.4.

document_sections.heading: Why the committee made the recommendation
document_sections.content: An NHS England safety report described instances of failure to remove emergency cerclage sutures, prompting the recommendation to plan and document their removal.

document_sections.heading: How the recommendation might affect practice
document_sections.content: The committee does not expect this recommendation to change practice.

document_sections.heading: Repeat courses of maternal corticosteroids
document_sections.content: The rationale and impact discussion concerns recommendations 1.9.4 to 1.9.6.

document_sections.heading: Why the committee made the recommendations
document_sections.content: Some evidence linked repeat maternal corticosteroid doses to lower birthweight. The absolute reduction was small, with a mean difference in birthweight of 114 g between women receiving repeat courses and those receiving one course. Subgroup analyses observed reductions when administration occurred below 30 weeks, intervals were less than 7 days, or the repeat course exceeded 24 mg in total. Birthweight also showed a significant downward trend as repeat-course numbers increased. There was no evidence of benefit for chronic lung disease; the committee was aware of a benefit in neonatal respiratory-support needs, an outcome not prioritised for the review. Good evidence found either no effect or beneficial effects on perinatal mortality, neonatal admission, intraventricular haemorrhage, growth at 2 years and neurodevelopmental delay. The committee considered one repeat course potentially beneficial if the earlier course was more than 7 days previously and preterm birth was imminent, but considered that birthweight effects might outweigh benefits with multiple repeat courses. Corticosteroids given for other reasons during pregnancy do not count toward the limit of 2 courses for preterm birth. Evidence is lacking for growth and neurodevelopment beyond 2 years and for the optimal repeat dose and interval, prompting further research.

document_sections.heading: How the recommendations might affect practice
document_sections.content: The guidance may reduce variation, increase use of one repeat course and decrease use of multiple courses, meaning more than 2. The committee expects little cost impact because a course is inexpensive and the eligible population is relatively small.

document_sections.heading: Context
document_sections.content: Preterm birth is the largest single cause of neonatal mortality and morbidity in the UK. In England and Wales in 2012, over 52,000 babies, around 7.3% of live births, were born before 37+0 weeks of pregnancy. The UK preterm-birth rate had not fallen over the preceding 10 years. Neonatal and infant mortality are high after preterm birth, with mortality risk increasing at earlier gestations; survivors also have higher disability rates. Recent UK studies comparing birth cohorts from 1995 and 2006 reported improved survival, from 40% to 53%, for births between 22 and 26 weeks, while disability rates among survivors changed little. Neurodevelopmental disability is the main long-term consequence. Individual risk is greatest at the earliest gestations, but the population burden is greatest for births at 32 to 36 weeks, lower at 28 to 31 weeks and lowest below 28 weeks because of the numbers born in each group. Around 75% of preterm births follow preterm labour, with or without preceding P-PROM. Remaining preterm births are planned when considered beneficial for the fetus or mother, for example because of extreme fetal growth retardation or maternal pre-eclampsia. The guideline examines treatment for symptomatic preterm labour and planned early birth, as well as diagnosis in symptomatic women, many of whom will not ultimately give birth preterm despite clinical suspicion. It does not determine who should have medically indicated preterm birth or address diagnostic or predictive testing in asymptomatic women.
